label: rem:planck-length-share-vs-total
title: $\ell_P$ carries two meanings: the Reeb share $\hbar_q$ and the normalised total $\ell_P(q) \equiv 1$
html:
Remark. \ell_P carries two meanings: the Reeb share \hbar_q and the normalised total \ell_P(q) \equiv 1

The symbol \ell_P appears twice in this chapter with two different referents, and read carelessly the two look like a disagreement by a factor of t_P \approx 10.1. They are not in disagreement. One is a share and the other is the total.

The share. At a point p of the brane, the Planck information unit sets the minimal quantisable size of an information unit and scales it as \ell_P^{\mathrm{step}} \sim \hbar_q. What is being named is the fraction of one Reeb circuit traversed by a single application of the connection: the per-step share. The relation is a proportionality, not an equality, and \hbar_q enters it as a weight: it is the Reeb coefficient of the categorical Dirac operator, which is exactly what the Reeb coefficient identity establishes.

The total. After one Planck step, the discrete Planck step records the displacement as

  \ell_P(q) \;=\; \hbar_q \cdot t_P \;=\; \bigl(1-q^{-1}\bigr)\cdot\frac{q}{q-1} \;=\; 1 .

What is being named here is the normalised total: one full Reeb circuit, an angular displacement carrying no length scale, set to unity so that the transcendental period 2\pi never enters and the construction survives over a finite field.

Why the two are consistent

The Planck time is defined as the reciprocal of the Reeb share, t_P = 1/\hbar_q, so the product of share and reciprocal is the circuit by construction. Writing \hbar_q \approx 0.0991 and \ell_P \equiv 1 side by side asserts that a step covers about a tenth of a circuit and that the circuit is one unit: two compatible statements about the same flow, not two values for one quantity.

The defect the pairing exposes is notational. A single glyph is doing duty for a per-step fraction and for a normalised whole, and the notation register admits no symbol reuse of that kind. The two uses are separated by writing \ell_P^{\mathrm{step}} for the share and reserving \ell_P(q) for the total.

A third symbol for the same share circulates in the fluid-dynamics chapter, where \ell_q = (q-1)/q is written for what is here \ell_P^{\mathrm{step}}. Three names for one quantity is one more collision of the same kind; unifying them is a separate edit and is not made here.
